newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. power market debate inches forward.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. power market debate inches forward.

text.p: A clash of consumers against electric utility monopolies is slowly escalating on Capitol Hill as Congress considers whether to order states to give everyone a choice of power suppliers.
For manufacturers looking to slash their electricity bills, the aim is to build a groundswell of support for customer choice among homeowners, businesses and industry.
This week, a lobbying group for homeowners joined the bandwagon of school districts, retailers and commercial building owners who are pressing for customer choice.
At the same time, many utilities are still fighting to keep other power producers out of their service territories and hang on to regulated, guaranteed returns on investments.

"The high cost utilities are willing to spend an unlimited amount of money to make sure that nothing happens. That's an incredible force against us," said John Anderson, executive director of the Electricity Consumer Resource Council, which lobbies for big manufacturers.
As lawmakers consider taking on the $200 billion monopoly electricity business, they are holding hearing after hearing to shield themselves from enemies they may make along the way.

"The challenge is making sure we move from the current fully-regulated market to a more deregulated and competitive one without littering the path with angry consumers, bankrupt electric utilities and poor service," Alaska Republican Sen. Frank Murkowski said in a column in a Capitol Hill newspaper.
Congress begins a two-week break this weekend with customer choice bills introduced by two key lawmakers on hold.
Senate Energy Committee chairman Murkowski plans to continue a string of workshops on deregulation next month and his House counterparts are planning hearings around the country at the same time.
No legislation is expected to come up for debate in committees before June at the earliest, said Rep. Dan Schaefer, a Colorado Republican, who is leading the customer choice effort on the House side.

Although he held nine hearings on power market competition last year, House energy and power subcommittee chairman Schaefer said before taking up his bill he wants to hold more hearings in committee after the field hearings in April.

In the most recent Senate workshop, Senate Energy Committee chairman Murkowski, state commissioners, and federal regulators downplayed the crucial question of whether to impose a deregulation deadline on all states.
"A date certain...is not the only issue on the table," said Elizabeth Moler, chairwoman of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

She said Congress should focus on repealing laws that stifle competition between utilities and other power producers, and expand federal regulators' authority to approve expansions, order access to, and police the power grid.

Since several states, such as California, New York, and Pennsylvania, are already moving toward customer choice, state commissioners said the federal government should ensure that open market states can request other states deregulate their markets if their local utilities want to compete in the open states.

Setting a deregulation deadline, the mantra of Schaefer and manufacturers, could be harmful to consumers if states are unable to create the conditions for a truly competitive market in time, said Texas Public Utility Commissioner Rober Gee.

States may end up "having competition in name only" while conditions on the ground, such as limited transmission paths, let local utilities keep their market dominance, he said at a workshop Thursday.

Idaho Public Utilities Commissioner Marsha Smith said her hydropower-dependent state was concerned about the impact deregulation would have on the river system, which is tied into farming, water rights, land use, and wildlife protection.
"Addressing these complex issues may take more time and resources than the federal government is willing to grant," Smith said in testimony for the workshop.
Even California, the first state to move toward customer choice, said states should act on their own.

"It appears clear that if there is to be federal legislation it should provide states with sufficient flexibility to address their own unique problems and concerns," said Greg Conlon, president of the California Public Utility Commission.

Murkowski is in favor of letting states set their own pace. "Unless and until it can be proven states are not acting in their consumers' interest, I see no reason for the federal government to step in and basically override the states."
But Schaefer told Reuters he would stick with his effort to set a deadline, although the actual date was negotiable from his proposal of December 15, 2000.
He said the threat of a mandate hovering over states since last year had forced them to contemplate opening their power markets to competition.
"Putting down in black and white what we'd like to do has really generated the debate out there," he said.
